title: After a 12.6% Monsoon Shortfall, India's Reservoirs Run Low as Super El Niño Looms
excerpt: The weakest monsoon in eleven years has left reservoirs below average and drought declarations in three states — with a super El Niño set to peak in December.
body:
• India's 2026 southwest monsoon ended 12.6% below normal — 759.4 mm against a long-period average of 868.6 mm — the first deficient monsoon since 2015 and the weakest in more than a decade.
  • The country's 178 major reservoirs stood at just ~70% of capacity in late September, against a 10-year average of 76.6%, and drought has been declared in Maharashtra, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh.
  • With a super El Niño expected to peak in December and linger into February 2027, economists warn of lower farm output, weaker rural demand and higher food inflation through 2027.
  • What this means for you: families in India should expect pressure on food prices and possible drinking-water rationing in cities this winter; NRIs supporting rural relatives may want to plan for a tighter rabi season.

India is running short of water, and the shortfall is deeper than the headline rainfall numbers suggest. The 2026 southwest monsoon ended 12.6% deficient — 759.4 mm of rain against a long-period average of 868.6 mm — the first deficient monsoon since 2015, the weakest in more than a decade, the fourth-lowest since 2001 and the 13th driest since 1901, according to India Meteorological Department data compiled by DSIJ. And with a super El Niño building in the Pacific, the worst may still be ahead.

A lopsided monsoon

The deficit was not evenly spread. East and Northeast India received 26% less rain than normal and the southern peninsula 24% less, while June — the sowing month — ran 36% below normal. July briefly recovered to 1% above normal before August slipped 14–16% short and September 8% short. That pattern matters: a strong July cannot undo a failed June for farmers who plant by the calendar, and a weak September leaves reservoirs short of the top-up they need before the dry season.

The reservoir picture confirms the damage. A Central Water Commission bulletin dated September 24 put the country's 178 major reservoirs at about 70% of capacity, against a 10-year average of 76.62%. Nomura estimates reservoirs were 28% short of full capacity at the end of September, and flagged extreme drought conditions in parts of Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab and Haryana. Drought declarations have been issued in Maharashtra, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh.

The El Niño multiplier

The World Meteorological Organization expects the current El Niño to peak in December 2026 and continue almost certainly into February 2027, and the IMD anticipates below-normal rainfall for October–December. Historically, El Niño suppresses India's winter rains and saps soil moisture just as farmers sow the rabi crop — wheat, pulses and oilseeds that feed the country through spring.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, speaking at an Asia Society event in New York, warned that geopolitical conflicts are already causing "significant fertilizer shortages" and that with a super El Niño, "a major food crisis" is coming in the months ahead. The World Bank has said the larger-than-expected monsoon deficit points to lower agricultural output, weaker rural demand and higher food inflation.

"With a super El Niño, a major food crisis is coming in the months ahead."

— S. Jaishankar, External Affairs Minister, at the Asia Society, New York

The economic fallout

The forecasts are sobering. S&P Global Market Intelligence expects India's rural economy to slow materially through 2026 and 2027. Morgan Stanley projects agricultural GVA growth of just 1.6% in FY27, down from the roughly 3.5% pace of the past three years. The pressure points are rabi sowing, sugarcane yields, winter crops, drinking-water rationing in cities and rising electricity demand as farmers pump harder from falling groundwater.

For the diaspora, the transmission channels are familiar: food inflation that eats into remittance value for rural families, weaker rural demand that drags on the consumption story many NRI investors own through Indian equities, and the perennial summer anxiety over water in cities from Chennai to Bengaluru. Analysts tracking the crisis note that the combination of a weak monsoon and a peaking El Niño is the worst pairing in a decade.

What's next

The next markers are the October–December rainfall numbers, the progress of rabi sowing, and reservoir levels at the start of the calendar year — the buffer India will carry into the hot, dry months of 2027. If the El Niño peaks as forecast, water rationing in major cities and a food-inflation spike are the scenarios to watch. For now, the monsoon that failed in June has left the country with the thinnest margin of safety it has had in eleven years.
